Fireside chat held two days before the FY2020 earnings release (March 11, 2021); no prepared remarks, all content in Q&A; company has no public financial targets.
Celsius framed as beneficiary of a structural 'seismic shift' toward healthy, functional energy within a still-growing global energy category.

Despite COVID shutting the fitness/specialty channel (~20% of revenue), Celsius recaptured volume in grocery, mass, drug and e-commerce — record revenues each quarter without losing sales, validating its 'more than an energy drink / daily lifestyle' thesis.
Celsius reached #3 on Amazon (just 0.02 points below Red Bull) and grabbed over 1% category share on trailing-4-week Nielsen data.
Input-cost inflation the principal headwind — aluminum can shortage plus rising freight/import costs/tariffs push gross margin to low-40s, expected to improve through H2 2021 and into 2022.
Can issue characterized as short-term and a competitive advantage given Celsius's global sourcing ability; new US can capacity coming online H2 2021/2022.
Convenience channel (~70% of energy volume) is the biggest opportunity, activated via the ~147-distributor DSD network in the 2021 beverage season.
DSD model has margin puts-and-takes — a margin share to the distributor offset by freight savings (full truckloads), removal of warehouse bill-backs, and higher velocity from cold placement.
Adding flavors/SKUs does not cannibalize — sales increase at an increasing rate (the 'billboard effect'); no single flavor dominates.
Operating leverage to come from gross profit improvement plus SG&A leverage on investments already made; following Monster's early-day algorithm; no public EBITDA targets.
China licensing/royalty model has an escalating five-year minimum royalty becoming a permanent floor, with upside participation thereafter.
FAST protein bars planned for US launch in 2021 via digital/e-commerce; HEAT and BCAA lines a matter of timing/sequencing; hard seltzer not a near-term priority.
Asked what is driving energy drink category momentum (up high single digits over 52 weeks despite COVID) and key future growth drivers.

Category grown mid-to-high single digits in NA for years; early pandemic dips reversed as consumers found energy drinks via delivery, Amazon, e-commerce and big-box. New consumers (Millennials, Gen Z), larger population entering, consumers not aging out, and busier lifestyles driving demand for functional better-for-you energy.
Asked what is driving the functional energy category to grow faster (~11% CAGR through 2023) than the broader energy category.

Described a 'seismic shift' toward healthy functional products — growth from new consumers, more global households buying consumables, more females entering a historically 18-24-male category. Positioned Celsius (50/50 male/female, 8+ vitamins, green tea, ginger, no sugar/crash/jitter) as the must-add offering.
Asked how Celsius differentiates to maintain/drive share gains given low entry barriers and increasing competitor focus.

Barriers to entry low (slightly higher now from the can shortage) but barriers to staying power very high — only ~1% of ~5,000 new brands annually reach $10M sales, ~1% of those reach $100M. Differentiation is authenticity (born in gyms/health clubs), clinically proven thermogenic functionality, healthy ingredients, and great taste.
Asked how Celsius's strong (sometimes triple-digit) track-channel trajectory will evolve as the economy reopens.

Watching closely; Celsius #3 on Amazon (0.02 points below Red Bull), turns faster than leading brands with equal placement. Despite ~20% of revenue from the closed fitness/specialty channel, validated its daily-lifestyle thesis by recapturing volume in online/grocery/mass/drug — record revenues without losing sales. Next focus is convenience (~70% of energy volume) via DSD.
Fitness channel recovery: incremental or shift
Asked whether the health/fitness channel recovery is just a volume shift or incremental growth in a post-vaccinated economy.

Recovery would be incremental — growth across Amazon, walmart.com, target.com, Instacart and traditional retail with better placements and expanded shelf space. Cited recent Nielsen data showing Celsius over 1% category share on a trailing-4-week basis.
Asked to unpack 2020 growth drivers — same-store sales vs. incremental distribution vs. innovation vs. e-commerce.

First-nine-months 2020 growth mainly grocery, mass, online and drug, with strong same-store sales as placements improved (~2-3 years to optimize a retailer). Some accounts being transitioned to DSD to speed that. Noted out-of-stocks at key accounts through warehouses/wholesalers, and bullish fitness distributors anticipating pent-up demand.
Asked where Celsius stands on DSD penetration and where the percentage of business on DSD will be by year-end 2021 / into 2022.

~147 distributors at end-Q3 2020 with ~30% of retail DSD-serviced as of end-September 2020, expected to increase through Q4 and 2021. Ongoing transitions with Target, CVS, Rite Aid and Meijer; all retail anticipated to transition over — a high priority — but no specific timeline stated.
Asked whether there are gross-to-operating-margin puts and takes when shifting an account to a DSD model.

There is a margin share to the distributor, offset by cost savings — improved freight (full truckloads vs. LTL), removal of warehouse bill-backs, and higher velocity from cold placement plus access to 100,000-150,000 independent convenience stores unreachable without DSD.
Asked how innovation contributes to 2021 and what the innovation pipeline looks like.

Retail scan data shows adding flavors/SKUs does not cannibalize — sales increase at an increasing rate (the 'billboard effect'), no single flavor dominates. New flavors planned for summer 2021, taken coast-to-coast via the DSD network with key-account partnerships and activation.
Asked how to think about input-cost inflation, can shortages and freight, and whether Celsius can take pricing to offset.

Taking front-line price is under evaluation but other levers preferred. Imported-can freight, import costs and tariffs (plus expensive Q1 can-wrapping) push gross margin to the low 40s, improving through H2 2021 and into 2022. Framed the can shortage as short-term and a competitive advantage; warehousing cans with adequate supply.
Asked the key areas of marketing spend and whether spend will rise with sales growth.

Methodical, ROI-positive marketing algorithm (experiential and social activation). As a percentage of revenue, marketing spend not expected to change, though absolute spend rises with revenue; reiterated driving profitable growth.
Asked where, from top-line to bottom-line, Celsius can extract operating leverage to grow earnings.

Operating leverage from gross profit enhancements plus SG&A leverage on investments already made (sales staff, marketing, logistics, accounting). Following Monster's early-day algorithm, expecting more EBITDA as a larger percentage at inflection points; no public targets.
Asked how e-commerce margins compare to brick-and-mortar and what mix of the business is e-commerce.
E-commerce margins very comparable to the rest of the business. E-commerce was ~20% of total revenue in Q3 2020, primarily from one customer (Amazon).
Asked about Celsius's international exposure, unique market agreements, and the longer-term opportunity.

Same seismic trends apply globally. Europe includes the Nordic operations (~8.5% Sweden share, Finland distribution, Norway growth) with methodical UK/Germany opportunities. Asia includes the China licensing/royalty agreement, Hong Kong, and a Malaysia partner (~2,000 locations), with Singapore and the Philippines under evaluation. North America remains the biggest near-term opportunity.
Asked to clarify the China licensing agreement — whether it is a capped royalty for five years and the upside if the brand keeps growing.

Confirmed a minimum royalty (detailed in the investor presentation) escalating each year for five years, becoming a permanent floor thereafter; as revenues grow the royalty becomes more accretive, allowing Celsius to participate in future category growth in China.
Asked about innovation/portfolio outside the energy drink space and its importance.

Non-core portfolio includes CELSIUS HEAT, the BCAA recovery line, and On-the-Go powder sticks (growing, at Walmart). Highlighted the Finland-based FAST protein snack portfolio and the plan to bring FAST bars (low-sugar, high-protein) to the US in 2021 via digital/e-commerce.
Asked about the HEAT product (vs. Rain/Bang), whether Celsius pulled back, and whether it could become a greater portfolio emphasis.

HEAT (same MetaPlus formula, enhanced caffeine) competes in the 300mg performance-energy category, focused on gyms/health clubs. Timing and sequencing key — core Celsius is at great velocity, the team must stay focused on distribution and fair share before re-emphasizing HEAT and the BCAA recovery line.
Relayed audience questions on whether Celsius would enter the hard seltzer space and whether it has the right brand equity.

Hard seltzer has come up in innovation meetings and the category is expanding, but it is not a current area of interest — Celsius could potentially bring a 'healthy seltzer' down the road, but the team must stay focused now.
Asked Fieldly to speak to key-account wins and Celsius's performance in those accounts.

Key accounts have gone well — with COVID delaying convenience expansion, Celsius focused on optimizing key accounts (Kroger Texas displays/cooler placement, Publix South Florida cold placement) where velocity improved markedly. Celsius turns better than the leading brand with the right placement. Speedway 2,700-store win had two flavors authorized with more planned; convenience (~70% of energy sales) is the target ahead.
